sense: awareness: without my knowledge, to my knowledge
also: to the best of my knowledge

terms.grammar: ablative absolute with īnsciēns, īnscientis, not knowing; likewise tē, eō īnsciente
evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.2.3: nihil … mē īnsciente esse factum
Plaut. Trin. 167: mē apsente atque īnsciente

terms.gloss: without the knowledge of, behind someone’s back
terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 98: haec clam mē omnia
Caes. BC 2.32.8, with the ablative: clam vōbīs
terms.comment: As a preposition, the Latin of comedy; classical prose uses clam as an adverb, “secretly” (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: to my knowledge, as far as I know
knowingly, with full knowledge, on purpose
terms.grammar: present participle of sciō, used as an adjective
evidence: Plaut. Poen. 112: dissimulat sciēns sē scīre

phrases.latin: tantum tē suspicārī volō, nihil in eā rē per conlēgam meum mē īnsciente esse factum
phrases.english: I only want you to suspect that nothing in that business was done by my colleague without my knowledge

phrases.latin: mē apsente atque īnsciente, incōnsultū meō
phrases.english: while I was away, without my knowledge, without asking me

phrases.latin: et is omnīs linguās scit, sed dissimulat sciēns sē scīre
phrases.english: and he knows every language, but knowingly pretends that he does not

sources: Lewis & Short: insciens · Lewis & Short: clam · Lewis & Short: scio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 337, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).
Cicero (Fam. 5.2.3, Ac. 2.146), Plautus (Trin. 167, Poen. 112), Terence (Heaut. 98) and Caesar (BC 2.32.8) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Plautus and Terence are quoted in the spelling of the Perseus texts (apsente, omnīs).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
